gloss: scorched rice crust; crispy rice at the bottom of the pot

definitions.gloss: scorched rice crust; crispy rice at the bottom of the pot
definitions.explanation: The thin, crispy layer of rice that forms at the bottom of a pot or rice cooker when rice is cooked over direct heat. Considered a delicacy in many cuisines.

examples.japanese: お{焦|こ}げ⟦が→が：00051_ga⟧⟦{好|す}き→好き：02355_suki⟧です。
examples.english: I like the crispy rice crust.

examples.japanese: ⟦{土鍋|どなべ}→土鍋：07949_donabe⟧⟦で→で：00502_de⟧⟦{炊|た}く→炊く：02127_taku⟧⟦と→と：00512_to⟧⟦{美味|おい}しい→美味しい：00740_oishii⟧お{焦|こ}げ⟦が→が：00051_ga⟧⟦できる→できる：00557_dekiru⟧。
examples.english: When you cook rice in a clay pot, you get delicious scorched rice.

examples.japanese: お{焦|こ}げ⟦に→に：00314_ni⟧⟦お{茶|ちゃ}→お茶：00576_ocha⟧⟦を→を：00422_wo⟧⟦かけて→かける：00854_kakeru⟧⟦{食|た}べる→食べる：00396_taberu⟧⟦の→の：09472_no⟧⟦が→が：00051_ga⟧⟦{祖母|そぼ}→祖母：00813_sobo⟧⟦の→の：09472_no⟧⟦{楽|たの}しみ→楽しみ：01651_tanoshimi⟧だった。
examples.english: Pouring tea over the scorched rice and eating it was my grandmother's little pleasure.

notes:
The お is an honorific/beautifying prefix attached to {焦|こ}げ (burnt part), from the verb ⟦{焦|こ}げる→焦げる：05344_kogeru⟧ (to scorch, to burn). Also written as おこげ in hiragana. The kanji form {御焦|おこ}げ is rarely used.

COMMON COLLOCATIONS:
- お{焦|こ}げ⟦が→が：00051_ga⟧⟦できる→できる：00557_dekiru⟧ (for scorched rice to form)
- お{焦|こ}げ⟦に→に：00314_ni⟧⟦お{湯|ゆ}→お湯：02518_oyu⟧⟦を→を：00422_wo⟧⟦かける→かける：00854_kakeru⟧ (to pour hot water over scorched rice)
- ⟦{土鍋|どなべ}→土鍋：07949_donabe⟧⟦の→の：09472_no⟧お{焦|こ}げ (clay pot scorched rice)
- パリパリ⟦の→の：09472_no⟧お{焦|こ}げ (crispy scorched rice)

SIMILAR WORDS:
- {焦|こ}げ — burnt part, scorch; the general term without the honorific prefix, can refer to any burnt food
- ⟦{焦|こ}げ{目|め}→焦げ目：08576_kogeme⟧ — browned surface, grill marks; the intentional browning on food
- ⟦{煎餅|せんべい}→煎餅：04958_senbei⟧ — rice cracker; a separate snack made from rice

CULTURAL NOTE:
In traditional Japanese cooking with ⟦{釜|かま}→釜：03880_kama⟧ (iron pots) or ⟦{土鍋|どなべ}→土鍋：07949_donabe⟧ (clay pots), お{焦|こ}げ was a natural byproduct. Many people consider it a treat. A classic way to enjoy it is お{焦|こ}げ{湯|ゆ} — pouring hot water or tea over the crispy rice to make a simple, comforting drink-food.
